## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, government, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a legal or regulatory question, firecrawl_gov_search searches primary law and regulatory material from US federal, state, and local government sources: statutes, regulations, codes, court opinions, and other government publications; firecrawl_search with categories: ["gov"] reaches the same sources in the web group and cannot be combined with other categories. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools are read-only and return ranked results. Billing: web, developer, and research search are billed per request; government search is free; Alexandria discovery (firecrawl_search with sources ["alexandria"] alone, and firecrawl_find_tools) is free; firecrawl_scrape is billed, as a page retrieval in url mode or at each executed capability's listed price in alexandria mode.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects, scoped to the
caller's HeyGen account via OAuth bearer token.

## Available Tools

### Feedback
- **submit_feedback** — Submit feedback the user expressed, or a meaningful terminal
  HyperFrames failure observed after supported recovery failed. Use `source="user"` only
  for the user's statement and `source="agent"` for an agent observation. Submit once per
  issue; omit secrets, raw media, and unrelated conversation text. Expected "project still
  building" responses and redirects to local HyperFrames skills are normal product behavior,
  so they are not automatically reported as failures.

### Author / Edit
- **compose** — Author a new HyperFrames project or apply an edit to an existing
  one. Pass `project_id` from a previous tool call to continue editing the same
  project; leave it empty (or omit) to start a new one. Returns immediately while
  the agent runs in the background (typically a few minutes). An optional
  `design_source` argument picks the brand style: a new project defaults to one of the
  vetted looks (`claude`, `blockframe`, or `monochrome`), with `mat` and `signal` also
  available as built-in presets. The compose response names the style that was applied and
  lists the alternatives, so a first video — when the user hasn't expressed a style
  preference — is a natural moment to let them know a different look is one follow-up
  away. On a follow-up edit, leaving `design_source` out keeps the project's current
  style; it's passed on an edit only to deliberately reskin.

### Read
- **list_projects** — List the caller's projects, newest first. Cursor-paginated

16	                                         Introduction
17	                                              An athlete’s health and availability to train and compete at an optimal performance
18	                                         level is a growing focus for professional sports organizations. Back-to-back competitions
19	                                         with limited recovery time, along with travelling across multiple time zones, are inherent
20	                                         challenges [1]. Studies suggest that a higher rate of injuries are sustained during the
21	                                         pre-season and during competitions [2]. These injuries include, but are not limited to,
22	                                         muscle strains [3], tendinopathies [4], and injuries to bone [1,5]. Athletic injuries can
23	                                         be challenging to treat in-season, with unpredictable healing times following treatment
24	                                         interventions. Surgical management is typically reserved for off-season athletes, as recovery
25	                                         commonly requires a substantial rehabilitation period of 6 to 9 months post-operatively [4].
26	                                         Identifying methods to treat injuries that exert positive clinical effects within 3 months
27	                                         would be desirable for in-season athletes. Emerging research suggests that extracorporeal
28	                                         shockwave therapy (ESWT) may represent an effective treatment to address sports-related
29	                                         injuries for in-season athletes and accelerate return to play.
30	
31	                                         What Is ESWT?
32	                                              Shockwaves are a type of energy that has biological effects at cellular, tissue, and
33	                                         organ levels. Some of the proposed mechanisms of action for ESWT include increased
34	                                         collagen synthesis [6], cellular proliferation and wound healing [7,8], pain reduction [9],
35	Citation: Rhim, H.C.; Borg-Stein, J.;    and neovascularization [10]. ESWT currently has two primary modes of delivery: radial
36	Sampson, S.; Tenforde, A.S. Utilizing
37	                                         shockwave therapy (R-SWT) and focused shockwave therapy (F-SWT). R-SWT generates
38	Extracorporeal Shockwave Therapy
39	                                         pressure waves that reach lower speeds and have lower peak pressure and therefore work
40	for in-Season Athletes. Healthcare
41	                                         on more superficial structures. On the other hand, F-SWT has the capacity to achieve
42	2023, 11, 1006. https://doi.org/
43	                                         deeper penetration from the site of application [11]. While both forms of ESWT have been
44	10.3390/healthcare11071006
45	                                         used to treat a variety of conditions, the differences in their mechanistic effects may lead to
46	Received: 7 March 2023                   different outcomes for a given condition.
47	Accepted: 30 March 2023                       ESWT has been shown to be effective in common athletic injuries, including plantar
48	Published: 1 April 2023                  fasciitis [12], Achilles tendinopathy [13], medial tibial stress syndrome [14], and proximal
49	                                         hamstring tendinopathy [15]. Some of the potential side effects include post-procedural
50	                                         pain, skin erythema, skin bruising, hematoma formation, nerve irritation, and superficial
51	                                         edema [11]. ESWT has been known to be effective for the longitudinal management of
52	Copyright: © 2023 by the authors.
53	                                         musculoskeletal injuries and has a favorable safety profile, with recent work suggesting
54	Licensee MDPI, Basel, Switzerland.
55	                                         feasibility to support utilization of treatment in the care of in-season athletes.

65

71	
72	
73	
74	
75	                            of ESWT [16], suggesting its potential role in muscle recovery. A single session of F-
76	                            SWT was found to provide relief of pain, increase in force, and improve pain-associated
77	                            impairments to daily living following eccentric exercise-induced, delayed-onset muscle
78	                            soreness [17].
79	                                  Chronic injuries: Return to sport may be accelerated by the use of ESWT with medial
80	                            tibial stress syndrome and bone trauma.
81	                                  A prospective observational study evaluated athletes treated with a graded running
82	                            program and F-SWT over 9 weeks for medial tibial stress syndrome. The authors demon-
83	                            strated significantly faster time to full recovery, defined by running 18 min consecutively
84	                            without pain, compared to a graded running program alone [18]. A randomized controlled
85	                            trial in military cadets with medial tibial stress syndrome observed one session of F-SWT
86	                            and exercise program resulted in longer running capacity and improvement in pain at four
87	                            weeks [19].
88	                                  A randomized controlled trial investigated European football players with groin pain
89	                            with bone edema of the pubic bone (osteitis pubis). Visual analog scale for pain and Hip
90	                            Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score were significantly improved in the group
91	                            receiving ESWT at 1 and 3 months. The athletes who received ESWT were also able to
92	                            return to football significantly earlier (73.2 days vs. 102.6 days) [20].
93	                                  One randomized controlled trial in jumping athletes identified limited relief at one
94	                            week and no sustained benefit of 3 sessions of F-SWT for management of patellar tendinopa-
95	                            thy during the competitive season [21]. The authors attributed these findings possibly
96	                            to not adding other exercises or treatments such as eccentric training and not modifying
97	                            training or competitions.
98	
99	                            What Are the Advantages of ESWT over Alternative Injection Treatments Such as
100	                            Corticosteroids and Platelet-Rich Plasma?
101	                                 Corticosteroid injections may offer rapid relief, but may increase the risk of atrophy,
102	                            pain, and tendon or soft tissue rupture [22]. Furthermore, needle injection therapies in an
103	                            athlete have potential complications, including infection, bleeding, increased pain, and
104	                            prolonged recovery time [22,23]. Unlike these interventions, athletes may continue activities
105	                            as tolerated with ESWT [24]. R-SWT for acute muscle injuries was tolerated well by elite
106	                            European football players, even when applied on a daily basis [25]. Furthermore, while
107	                            F-SWT alone was not shown to be beneficial in jumping athletes, the athletes continued
108	                            to participate in both training and matches without noticeable adverse events during
109	                            treatment [21].
110	                                 Platelet-rich plasma is commonly used for sports medicine injuries given the mech-
111	                            anism of action to stimulate tissue healing, reduce pain, without concerns of cellular
112	                            toxicity [26]. A meta-analysis, including five randomized controlled trials, suggests that
113	                            the use of platelet-rich plasma may result in an earlier return to sport in the treatment of
114	                            acute grade I or II muscle strains, excluding those isolated to the hamstring muscle [27].
115	                            Despite this finding, based on the systematic review of post-procedure protocols following
116	                            platelet-rich plasma injections, weight bearing limitation or activity limitation has been
117	                            imposed immediately after the injection of platelet-rich plasma and up to 7 days and
118	                            return to play restricted up to 4-6 weeks [28]. A similar lack of clinical results is observed
119	                            in the management of acute hamstring injuries in competitive and recreational athletes
120	                            with intramuscular platelet-rich plasma [29]. However, this involved substandard platelet
121	                            concentration and dosage, limiting researchers to the conclusion that plasma concentrates
122	                            rather than platelet-rich plasma is ineffective for acute hamstring injuries.
123	
124	                            Clinical Applications and Future Work
125	                                 R-SWT is classified as a low-risk device with a good safety profile that can be used for
126	                            in-season athletes to facilitate their return to sport in selected injuries. The use of ESWT
127	                            may be favorable for in-season athletes following load management strategies to allow
128	 Healthcare 2023, 11, 1006                                                                                                             3 of 5
129	
130	
131	
132	
133	                                   for healing, or as a bridge for more advanced procedures such as platelet-rich plasma or
134	                                   surgery for off-season use.
135	                                        There are some case series and reports that support the use of ESWT on physically
136	                                   active or athletic populations with early outcomes for sports injuries including acute
137	                                   muscle injuries [25], myositis ossificans [30,31], plantar fasciitis [32], Achilles tendinosis [33],
138	                                   proximal hamstring tendinopathy [33], and non-union stress fractures [24,34]. Future high-
139	                                   quality studies should aim to capture larger cohorts of athletes as well as early outcomes
140	                                   such as 3 and 6 weeks, not limited to outcomes 12 weeks or beyond that have been
141	                                   commonly reported. ESWT should also be considered an adjunctive tool for managing
142	                                   commonly encountered athletic injuries. Future research will explore its combination with
143	                                   orthobiologics to help with perioperative and post-operative recovery, including anterior
144	                                   cruciate ligament reconstruction [35].
145	
146	                                   Conclusions
147	                                        ESWT offers the potential to accelerate recovery from athletic injury and save athletic
148	                                   clubs valuable resources. Further human athlete studies using ESWT on larger cohorts are
149	                                   needed to explore optimal indications, dosing, and frequency parameters.

                                         interventions. Surgical management is typically reserved for off-season athletes, as recovery
                                         commonly requires a substantial rehabilitation period of 6 to 9 months post-operatively [4].
                                         Identifying methods to treat injuries that exert positive clinical effects within 3 months
                                         would be desirable for in-season athletes. Emerging research suggests that extracorporeal
                                         shockwave therapy (ESWT) may represent an effective treatment to address sports-related
                                         injuries for in-season athletes and accelerate return to play.

                                         What Is ESWT?
                                              Shockwaves are a type of energy that has biological effects at cellular, tissue, and
                                         organ levels. Some of the proposed mechanisms of action for ESWT include increased
                                         collagen synthesis [6], cellular proliferation and wound healing [7,8], pain reduction [9],
Citation: Rhim, H.C.; Borg-Stein, J.;    and neovascularization [10]. ESWT currently has two primary modes of delivery: radial
Sampson, S.; Tenforde, A.S. Utilizing

                            of ESWT [16], suggesting its potential role in muscle recovery. A single session of F-
                            SWT was found to provide relief of pain, increase in force, and improve pain-associated
                            impairments to daily living following eccentric exercise-induced, delayed-onset muscle
                            soreness [17].
                                  Chronic injuries: Return to sport may be accelerated by the use of ESWT with medial
                            tibial stress syndrome and bone trauma.
                                  A prospective observational study evaluated athletes treated with a graded running
                            program and F-SWT over 9 weeks for medial tibial stress syndrome. The authors demon-
                            strated significantly faster time to full recovery, defined by running 18 min consecutively
                            without pain, compared to a graded running program alone [18]. A randomized controlled
                            trial in military cadets with medial tibial stress syndrome observed one session of F-SWT
                            and exercise program resulted in longer running capacity and improvement in pain at four
                            weeks [19].
                                  A randomized controlled trial investigated European football players with groin pain
                            with bone edema of the pubic bone (osteitis pubis). Visual analog scale for pain and Hip
                            Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score were significantly improved in the group
                            receiving ESWT at 1 and 3 months. The athletes who received ESWT were also able to
                            return to football significantly earlier (73.2 days vs. 102.6 days) [20].
                                  One randomized controlled trial in jumping athletes identified limited relief at one
                            week and no sustained benefit of 3 sessions of F-SWT for management of patellar tendinopa-
                            thy during the competitive season [21]. The authors attributed these findings possibly
                            to not adding other exercises or treatments such as eccentric training and not modifying
                            training or competitions.

                            What Are the Advantages of ESWT over Alternative Injection Treatments Such as
                            Corticosteroids and Platelet-Rich Plasma?
                                 Corticosteroid injections may offer rapid relief, but may increase the risk of atrophy,
                            pain, and tendon or soft tissue rupture [22]. Furthermore, needle injection therapies in an
                            athlete have potential complications, including infection, bleeding, increased pain, and
                            prolonged recovery time [22,23]. Unlike these interventions, athletes may continue activities
                            as tolerated with ESWT [24]. R-SWT for acute muscle injuries was tolerated well by elite
                            European football players, even when applied on a daily basis [25]. Furthermore, while
                            F-SWT alone was not shown to be beneficial in jumping athletes, the athletes continued
                            to participate in both training and matches without noticeable adverse events during
                            treatment [21].
                                 Platelet-rich plasma is commonly used for sports medicine injuries given the mech-
                            anism of action to stimulate tissue healing, reduce pain, without concerns of cellular
                            toxicity [26]. A meta-analysis, including five randomized controlled trials, suggests that
                            the use of platelet-rich plasma may result in an earlier return to sport in the treatment of
                            acute grade I or II muscle strains, excluding those isolated to the hamstring muscle [27].
                            Despite this finding, based on the systematic review of post-procedure protocols following
                            platelet-rich plasma injections, weight bearing limitation or activity limitation has been
                            imposed immediately after the injection of platelet-rich plasma and up to 7 days and
                            return to play restricted up to 4-6 weeks [28]. A similar lack of clinical results is observed
                            in the management of acute hamstring injuries in competitive and recreational athletes
                            with intramuscular platelet-rich plasma [29]. However, this involved substandard platelet
                            concentration and dosage, limiting researchers to the conclusion that plasma concentrates
                            rather than platelet-rich plasma is ineffective for acute hamstring injuries.

                            Clinical Applications and Future Work
                                 R-SWT is classified as a low-risk device with a good safety profile that can be used for
                            in-season athletes to facilitate their return to sport in selected injuries. The use of ESWT
                            may be favorable for in-season athletes following load management strategies to allow
 Healthcare 2023, 11, 1006                                                                                                             3 of 5




                                   for healing, or as a bridge for more advanced procedures such as platelet-rich plasma or
                                   surgery for off-season use.
                                        There are some case series and reports that support the use of ESWT on physically
                                   active or athletic populations with early outcomes for sports injuries including acute
                                   muscle injuries [25], myositis ossificans [30,31], plantar fasciitis [32], Achilles tendinosis [33],
                                   proximal hamstring tendinopathy [33], and non-union stress fractures [24,34]. Future high-
                                   quality studies should aim to capture larger cohorts of athletes as well as early outcomes
                                   such as 3 and 6 weeks, not limited to outcomes 12 weeks or beyond that have been
                                   commonly reported. ESWT should also be considered an adjunctive tool for managing
                                   commonly encountered athletic injuries. Future research will explore its combination with
                                   orthobiologics to help with perioperative and post-operative recovery, including anterior
                                   cruciate ligament reconstruction [35].

                                   Conclusions
                                        ESWT offers the potential to accelerate recovery from athletic injury and save athletic
                                   clubs valuable resources. Further human athlete studies using ESWT on larger cohorts are
                                   needed to explore optimal indications, dosing, and frequency parameters.

Valid but Invalid: Suboptimal ImPACT Baseline
Performance in University Athletes


                                                                                                                                                      CLINICAL SCIENCES
SAMUEL R. WALTON1, DONNA K. BROSHEK2, JASON R. FREEMAN3, C. MUNRO CULLUM4, and JACOB E. RESCH1

                                                                       ABSTRACT
          WALTON, S. R., D. K. BROSHEK, J. R. FREEMAN, C. M. CULLUM, and J. E. RESCH. Valid but Invalid: Suboptimal ImPACT
          Baseline Performance in University Athletes. Med. Sci. Sports Exerc., Vol. 50, No. 7, pp. 1377–1384, 2018. Purpose: This study aimed to
          investigate the frequency of valid yet suboptimal Immediate Postconcussion Assessment and Cognitive Test (ImPACT) performance in
          university athletes and to explore the benefit of subsequent ImPACT administrations. Methods: This descriptive laboratory study
          involved baseline administration of ImPACT to 769 university athletes per the institution_s concussion management protocol. Testing
          was proctored in groups of e2 participants. Participants who scored below the 16th percentile according to ImPACT normative data were
          readministered the ImPACT test up to two additional times because these scores were thought to be potentially indicative of suboptimal
          effort or poor understanding of instructions. Descriptive analyses were used to examine validity indicators and individual Verbal and
          Visual Memory, Visual Motor Speed, and Reaction Time ImPACT composite scores in initial and subsequent administrations. Results:
          On the basis of ImPACT_s validity criteria, 1% (9/769) of administrations were invalid and 14.6% (112/769) had one or more composite
          score of G16th percentile but were considered valid. After one readministration, 71.4% (80/112) achieved scores of Q16th percentile
          and an additional 18 of 32 scored Q16th percentile after a third administration. Verbal Memory was most commonly G16th percentile on
          the first administration (43%), Verbal Memory and Visual Motor Speed on the second administration (44% each), and Visual Motor
          Speed alone on the third administration (50%). Conclusions: Approximately 16% of ImPACT records were flagged as invalid or had
          one or more composite scores of G16th percentile, potentially indicative of suboptimal performance. Upon readministration, 88% of those
          participants scored 916th percentile. Clinicians must be aware of suboptimal ImPACT performance as it limits the clinical utility of the
          baseline assessment. Further research is needed to address factors leading to ‘‘valid’’ but invalid baseline performance. Key Words:

1	Validation of a Composite Outcome Score
2	for Assessing Return to Sports After
3	Achilles Tendon Repair
4	Ronny Lopes,*y MD, Kinan Freiha,z MD , Michael R. Carmont,§ MD, Eugénie Valentin,z

10	Background: The Ankle-GO is a composite outcome score based on 4 functional tests and 2 patient-reported outcome meas-
11	ures. It was initially described and validated for its ability to predict return to sports (RTS) at the same level of play after lateral
12	ankle sprains.
13	Purpose/Hypothesis: The main aim of this study was to assess the psychometric properties of the Ankle-GO in patients after
14	Achilles tendon repair. The second objective was to evaluate its ability to predict RTS at the same level of play. It was hypoth-
15	esized that this composite outcome score is a valid and reliable tool that is able to discriminate and predict the level of RTS at 9
16	months after Achilles tendon repair.
17	Study Design: Case-control study; Level of evidence, 3.
18	Methods: This was a prospective multicenter study. Patients who were active in sports and underwent primary acute Achilles
19	tendon repair between April 2021 and December 2022 were included. A control group comprising 30 participants with no history
20	of lower limb injuries was also evaluated. After standard rehabilitation for the first 2 months, the Ankle-GO was administered at 6
21	and 9 months after repair by the same experienced physical therapist. During testing, the patients were asked whether they were
22	able to practice their main sport again and, if so, whether at the same or a lower level of play. A comparison between control
23	participants and patients at 9 months after surgery was performed.
24	Results: A total of 50 patients (24 women and 26 men), with a mean age of 38.3 6 10.1 years, were included. No patients were
25	lost to follow-up at 9 months. The Ankle-GO score at 6 months was 10.7 6 4.8. At 9 months, the score had risen by 4.8 points. All
26	participants scored above the minimum threshold. The minimum score achieved was 3 points (n = 5 [10%]). Only 1 patient (2%)
27	obtained the maximum score (25 points). There was a significant difference in the Ankle-GO score between patients at 6 and 9
28	months and between control participants and patients at 9 months after Achilles tendon repair. Of the 50 patients included in the
29	study, 14 (28%) returned to their preinjury level of sport at 9 months. The ability of the Ankle-GO score at 6 months to predict RTS
30	at the preinjury level at 9 months was good (area under the curve = 0.71 [95% CI, 0.56-0.85]; P \ .01). A Youden index of 0.42 was
31	observed for a cut-off score of 8 points, which corresponds to a sensitivity of 81.8% and a specificity of 41.2%.
32	Conclusion: The Ankle-GO is a valid tool to evaluate and discriminate patients during the RTS continuum after Achilles tendon
33	repair and to predict RTS at the same level at 9 months after surgery. This composite outcome score assesses ankle function and
34	the patient’s psychological readiness to avoid premature RTS and worsening of the injury. Further studies are needed to assess
35	its value in identifying and predicting patients at risk of a recurrence.
36	Keywords: Achilles tendon rupture; Achilles tendon repair; return to sports; Ankle-GO; psychological readiness

Validation of a Composite Outcome Score
for Assessing Return to Sports After
Achilles Tendon Repair
Ronny Lopes,*y MD, Kinan Freiha,z MD , Michael R. Carmont,§ MD, Eugénie Valentin,z
Kylian Alvino,|| PT, Mohamed Mousa,z MD , Gauthier Rauline,z PT,
Francxois Fourchet,{# PT, PhD, Brice Picot,#** PT, PhD , and Alexandre Hardy,z MD, PhD
Investigation performed at Centre Orthopédique Santy, Hôpital Privé Jean Mermoz,
Ramsay Santé, Lyon, France

Background: The Ankle-GO is a composite outcome score based on 4 functional tests and 2 patient-reported outcome meas-
ures. It was initially described and validated for its ability to predict return to sports (RTS) at the same level of play after lateral
ankle sprains.
Purpose/Hypothesis: The main aim of this study was to assess the psychometric properties of the Ankle-GO in patients after
Achilles tendon repair. The second objective was to evaluate its ability to predict RTS at the same level of play. It was hypoth-
esized that this composite outcome score is a valid and reliable tool that is able to discriminate and predict the level of RTS at 9
months after Achilles tendon repair.
Study Design: Case-control study; Level of evidence, 3.
Methods: This was a prospective multicenter study. Patients who were active in sports and underwent primary acute Achilles
tendon repair between April 2021 and December 2022 were included. A control group comprising 30 participants with no history
of lower limb injuries was also evaluated. After standard rehabilitation for the first 2 months, the Ankle-GO was administered at 6
and 9 months after repair by the same experienced physical therapist. During testing, the patients were asked whether they were
able to practice their main sport again and, if so, whether at the same or a lower level of play. A comparison between control
participants and patients at 9 months after surgery was performed.
Results: A total of 50 patients (24 women and 26 men), with a mean age of 38.3 6 10.1 years, were included. No patients were
lost to follow-up at 9 months. The Ankle-GO score at 6 months was 10.7 6 4.8. At 9 months, the score had risen by 4.8 points. All
participants scored above the minimum threshold. The minimum score achieved was 3 points (n = 5 [10%]). Only 1 patient (2%)
obtained the maximum score (25 points). There was a significant difference in the Ankle-GO score between patients at 6 and 9
months and between control participants and patients at 9 months after Achilles tendon repair. Of the 50 patients included in the
study, 14 (28%) returned to their preinjury level of sport at 9 months. The ability of the Ankle-GO score at 6 months to predict RTS
at the preinjury level at 9 months was good (area under the curve = 0.71 [95% CI, 0.56-0.85]; P \ .01). A Youden index of 0.42 was
observed for a cut-off score of 8 points, which corresponds to a sensitivity of 81.8% and a specificity of 41.2%.
Conclusion: The Ankle-GO is a valid tool to evaluate and discriminate patients during the RTS continuum after Achilles tendon
repair and to predict RTS at the same level at 9 months after surgery. This composite outcome score assesses ankle function and
the patient’s psychological readiness to avoid premature RTS and worsening of the injury. Further studies are needed to assess
its value in identifying and predicting patients at risk of a recurrence.
Keywords: Achilles tendon rupture; Achilles tendon repair; return to sports; Ankle-GO; psychological readiness

31	   ABSTRACT
32	   Consumer-­grade optical heart rate (HR) sensors emerged as promising tools to monitor volume and intensity of physical ac-
33	   tivity (PA). However, no validation study of optical HR sensors included recent comprehensive validation recommendations,
34	   required for facilitating usage for medical purposes. Validity of HR data measured with four consumer-­grade optical sensors, the
35	   wrist-­worn Garmin Venu 2S and Polar Vantage M2, and the upper arm-­worn Polar Verity Sense and Scosche Rhythm24 were
36	   assessed in 32 participants over 24 h including various laboratory-­based and free-­living activities. Furthermore, validity of time
37	   at moderate or vigorous PA intensity zones was analyzed. A medical-­grade ECG served as a reference. Reliability was assessed
38	   by analyzing data of laboratory-­based activities during two visits. Across activities, the mean absolute percentage error ranged
39	   from 2.2% to 4.7% and intraclass correlation coefficients ranged from 0.91 to 0.98, indicating high validity for all optical sensors.
40	   All sensors validly detected time spent at moderate or vigorous intensities (mean error < 10%), except Polar M2 for moderate PA
41	   (mean error 12.8%) and Garmin V2 for vigorous PA (mean error −15.9%). Sensor day-­to-­day reliability was high, indicated by a
42	   mean absolute error of < 5 beats/min. Upper arm-­worn sensors consistently outperformed wrist-­worn sensors, particularly in ac-
43	   tivities involving increased arm movement and at higher intensities. Our findings identified an overall high validity of these four
44	   consumer-­grade optical HR sensors, also for assessing time spent at higher PA intensities. However, differences were observed
45	   between sensors regarding activity subtypes and intensity levels. These data support informed decisions when selecting optical
46	   sensors for PA monitoring and intervention.

Validity of Four Consumer-­Grade Optical Heart Rate
Sensors for Assessing Volume and Intensity Distribution of
Physical Activity
Michael Neudorfer1    | Devender Kumar2                                | Jan David Smeddinck 2                   | Stefan Tino Kulnik 2 | Josef Niebauer1,2,3 |
Gunnar Treff 2,3   | Mahdi Sareban1,2

1University Institute of Sports Medicine, Prevention and Rehabilitation, University Hospital Salzburg, Paracelsus Medical University, Salzburg,

Austria | 2Ludwig Boltzmann Institute for Digital Health and Prevention, Salzburg, Austria | 3Institute of Molecular Sports and Rehabilitation Medicine,
Paracelsus Medical University, Salzburg, Austria

Correspondence: Mahdi Sareban (m.sareban@salk.at)

Received: 27 June 2024 | Revised: 4 September 2024 | Accepted: 14 October 2024

Funding: The authors received no specific funding for this work.

Keywords: Garmin | mHealth | physical activity | physical medicine and rehabilitation | polar | telemedicine | validation | wearables


   ABSTRACT
   Consumer-­grade optical heart rate (HR) sensors emerged as promising tools to monitor volume and intensity of physical ac-
   tivity (PA). However, no validation study of optical HR sensors included recent comprehensive validation recommendations,
   required for facilitating usage for medical purposes. Validity of HR data measured with four consumer-­grade optical sensors, the
   wrist-­worn Garmin Venu 2S and Polar Vantage M2, and the upper arm-­worn Polar Verity Sense and Scosche Rhythm24 were
   assessed in 32 participants over 24 h including various laboratory-­based and free-­living activities. Furthermore, validity of time
   at moderate or vigorous PA intensity zones was analyzed. A medical-­grade ECG served as a reference. Reliability was assessed
   by analyzing data of laboratory-­based activities during two visits. Across activities, the mean absolute percentage error ranged
   from 2.2% to 4.7% and intraclass correlation coefficients ranged from 0.91 to 0.98, indicating high validity for all optical sensors.
   All sensors validly detected time spent at moderate or vigorous intensities (mean error < 10%), except Polar M2 for moderate PA
   (mean error 12.8%) and Garmin V2 for vigorous PA (mean error −15.9%). Sensor day-­to-­day reliability was high, indicated by a
   mean absolute error of < 5 beats/min. Upper arm-­worn sensors consistently outperformed wrist-­worn sensors, particularly in ac-
   tivities involving increased arm movement and at higher intensities. Our findings identified an overall high validity of these four
   consumer-­grade optical HR sensors, also for assessing time spent at higher PA intensities. However, differences were observed
   between sensors regarding activity subtypes and intensity levels. These data support informed decisions when selecting optical
   sensors for PA monitoring and intervention.

   was prospectively registered at Clini​calTr​ials.​gov (ID NCT05525000).

                            Validity of Force–Velocity Proﬁling Assessed
                                 With a Pneumatic Leg Press Device
                          Kolbjørn Lindberg, Ingrid Eythorsdottir, Paul Solberg, Øyvind Gløersen,
                                  Olivier Seynnes, Thomas Bjørnsen, and Gøran Paulsen

     Purpose: The aim of this study was to examine the concurrent validity of force–velocity (FV) variables assessed across 5 Keiser
     leg press devices. Methods: A linear encoder and 2 independent force plates (MuscleLab devices) were mounted on each of the 5
     leg press devices. A total of 997 leg press executions, covering a wide range of forces and velocities, were performed by 14
     participants (29 [7] y, 181 [5] cm, 82 [8] kg) across the 5 devices. Average and peak force, velocity, and power values were
     collected simultaneously from the Keiser and MuscleLab devices for each repetition. Individual FV proﬁles were ﬁtted to each
     participant from peak and average force and velocity measurements. Theoretical maximal force, velocity, and power were
     deduced from the FV relationship. Results: Average and peak force and velocity had a coefﬁcient of variation of 1.5% to 8.6%,
     near-perfect correlations (.994–.999), and a systematic bias of 0.7% to 7.1% when compared with reference measurements.
     Average and peak power showed larger coefﬁcient of variations (11.6% and 17.2%), despite excellent correlations (.977 and
     .952), and trivial to small biases (3.9% and 8.4%). Extrapolated FV variables showed near-perfect correlations (.983–.997) with
     trivial to small biases (1.4%–11.2%) and a coefﬁcient of variation of 1.4% to 5.9%. Conclusions: The Keiser leg press device can
     obtain valid measurements over a wide range of forces and velocities across different devices. To accurately measure power,
     theoretical maximal power calculated from the FV proﬁle is recommended over average and peak power values from single
     repetitions, due to the lower random error observed for theoretical maximal power.

     Keywords: strength testing, athlete assessment, force plate, linear encoder

{
 "id":"Q36",
 "sourceFile":"Valid but Invalid- Suboptimal ImPACT Baseline Performance in University Athletes.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title 'Valid but Invalid: Suboptimal ImPACT Baseline Performance in University Athletes' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Methodological / Validation Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Brain Health & Psychology","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Athletic Training","Sports Medicine","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Female Athletes","Collegiate"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Descriptive laboratory study of baseline ImPACT tests in 760 NCAA Division I student-athletes at one university, after 9 records were flagged invalid by ImPACT's own criteria. Athletes with any composite score below the 16th percentile were retested up to two more times; 112 of 760 (14.7%) had at least one such score at first baseline, and 80 of those 112 (71.4%) reached the 16th percentile or higher after one retest. Valid-but-invalid athletes scored lower on Verbal Memory, Visual Memory and Visual Motor Speed, and higher on Reaction Time, at first baseline.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Single university, one ImPACT version and proctoring in pairs, with no stand-alone effort measure, so the cause of low first scores cannot be confirmed. The abstract reports 769 athletes and about 16% flagged, while the results analyse 760 athletes and give 14.7% (112/760) and 13% (98/760); the counts conflict and this is noted in limitations.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the roughly 15% low-score rate as a general measure of how often baselines are wrong, when it comes from one university, one test version and a retest pattern that may reflect practice or effort rather than true ability.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2018,
   "citation":"Walton SR, Broshek DK, Freeman JR, Cullum CM, Resch JE. Valid but Invalid: Suboptimal ImPACT Baseline Performance in University Athletes. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2018;50(7):1377-1384.",
   "doi":"10.1249/MSS.0000000000001592",
   "abstract":"Baseline ImPACT was given to 769 university athletes. Athletes scoring below the 16th percentile on any composite were retested up to two more times. Nine tests (1%) were invalid, and 14.6% had a composite score below the 16th percentile despite passing validity checks. After one retest, 71.4% of those athletes reached the 16th percentile or higher, and 88% did so after a third test.",
   "tldr":"About 1% of ImPACT baselines were invalid, and about 15% had a low composite score that still passed ImPACT's validity checks. Most low scores rose on retest, so a low baseline should be repeated before it is used as the comparison point after injury.",
   "methods":"Baseline ImPACT was given to Division I student-athletes in groups of no more than two, with an athletic trainer trained in ImPACT administering the test. Athletes with any composite below the 16th percentile were retested no earlier than 7 days later, and up to a third time if still low. Composite scores across baseline 1, 2 and 3 were compared with paired t-tests and ImPACT's reliable change index.",
   "findings":"Of 769 records, 9 were flagged invalid by ImPACT. Of the 760 valid profiles, 112 (14.7%) had at least one composite below the 16th percentile at baseline 1. Of those, 80 (71.4%) reached the 16th percentile or higher on baseline 2, and 18 of the 32 still low at baseline 2 did so at baseline 3. The valid-but-invalid group improved significantly on Verbal Memory, Visual Memory, Visual Motor Speed and Reaction Time across retests.",
   "limitations":"Single university, no stand-alone measure of effort, and no record of prior ImPACT exposure. The reported counts conflict: the abstract gives 769 athletes and about 16% flagged, while the results analyse 760 athletes with 14.7% (112/760) and 13% (98/760) low. Many retests fell during the season, so training effects cannot be excluded.",
   "practicalImplications":"Check ImPACT's validity indicators and composite percentiles at baseline. When any composite falls below the 16th percentile, repeat the test before accepting that baseline as the comparison point.",
   "athleteDev":"Run baseline cognitive testing in a controlled, proctored session. Repeat any low composite before accepting it as the athlete's baseline, since many first low scores rose on retest.",
   "rtp":"Relevant to return to sport only through the baseline comparison after a concussion. The study cannot show whether any individual baseline is accurate, so it cannot support a return-to-play decision on its own."
 }
}

{

 "sourceFile":"Validation of a Composite Outcome Score for Assessing Return to Sports After Achilles Tendon Repair.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",

 "studyDesign":"Methodological / Validation Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Rehabilitation & Return to Sport","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Rehabilitation","Sports Medicine","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Female Athletes","Injured Athletes","Professional / Elite","Adult / Recreational","Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Prospective three-centre study of the Ankle-GO composite return-to-sport score in 50 patients (mean age 38.3 years) who were active in sport, tested at 6 and 9 months after primary Achilles tendon repair, with 30 uninjured controls. The score rose from 10.7 at 6 months to 15.5 at 9 months, with no floor or ceiling effects and a Cronbach alpha of 0.78. At 9 months, 14 of 50 patients (28%) had returned to their preinjury level, and a 6-month cut-off of 8 points gave sensitivity of 81.8% and specificity of 41.2% (AUC 0.71).",
 "screeningLimitations":"A 50-patient sample at three centres in France, of whom only 8% were professional athletes, with 9-month follow-up only. Test-retest reliability was not assessed in this population, and only 14 patients returned to preinjury level, so the prediction rests on few events. The text gives 24 women and 26 men, while Table 2 gives 24 male and 30 female patients; this conflict is noted.",
 "synthesisCaution":"The 8-point cut-off comes from one sample and has low specificity (41%), so staff could treat it as a clearance threshold when it only flags a weak prediction of same-level return.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Lopes R, Freiha K, Carmont MR, Valentin E, Alvino K, Mousa M, et al. Validation of a Composite Outcome Score for Assessing Return to Sports After Achilles Tendon Repair. Am J Sports Med. 2025:1-9.",
   "doi":"10.1177/03635465251333142",
   "abstract":"The Ankle-GO composite score (four functional tests and two patient-reported measures) was tested in 50 patients at 6 and 9 months after Achilles tendon repair, with 30 controls. The score improved from 6 to 9 months and differed from controls at 9 months. The 6-month score predicted same-level return to sport at 9 months with fair to good discrimination (AUC 0.71). Only 28% of patients returned to their preinjury level.",
   "tldr":"In 50 patients after Achilles tendon repair, the Ankle-GO score rose from 10.7 at 6 months to 15.5 at 9 months. Only 28% had returned to preinjury sport by 9 months, and a 6-month cut-off of 8 points predicted same-level return with 82% sensitivity but only 41% specificity.",
   "methods":"Prospective multicentre study following COSMIN guidance. The Ankle-GO (single-leg stance, modified star excursion, side hop and figure-of-8 hop tests, plus FAAM and ALR-RSI) was given at 6 and 9 months after open primary repair. Floor and ceiling effects, internal consistency, structural and discriminant validity were assessed, and the 6-month score was used in an ROC analysis to predict same-level return at 9 months.",
   "findings":"The Ankle-GO rose from 10.7 to 15.5 between 6 and 9 months (P < .0001), and 9-month scores differed from controls. No floor or ceiling effects were seen, and internal consistency was 0.78. The 6-month score predicted same-level return with AUC 0.71 (95% CI 0.56-0.85); the cut-off of 8 gave sensitivity 81.8% and specificity 41.2%.",
   "limitations":"Test-retest reliability and statistical components were not assessed in this population; the authors judged retesting during rehabilitation inappropriate. The sex counts conflict between the text (24 women, 26 men) and Table 2 (24 male, 30 female). Few patients returned to preinjury level, and the tool's value for identifying re-rupture risk is untested.",

{
 "id":"Q38",
 "sourceFile":"Validity and reliability of Strive Sense 3 for muscle activity monitoring during the squat exercise.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title 'Validity and Reliability of Strive Sense3 for Muscle Activity Monitoring During the Squat Exercise' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Methodological / Validation Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Research & Analytics","Coaching"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Within-subjects validation of the Strive Sense3 smart-textile sEMG shorts against a Noraxon research-grade system, recording rectus femoris activity during back squats at 30%, 60% and 80% of estimated 1RM. Seventeen recreationally trained adults (12 men, 5 women) were tested; data from participant 14 and participant 3's medium and heavy trials were excluded. Correlation was good or better in 93% of trials, and reliability was good or better in 87% of absolute and 98% of normalised sEMG trials, with better agreement at medium and heavy loads.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The sample was recreationally trained adults, not athletes, tested in one laboratory session at a 21.33 Hz sampling rate rather than the device's 1000 Hz capability. Outliers were linked to poor electrode contact and shorts fit. Five basketball coaches add an autoethnographic commentary, and one author has a former student now employed by Strive.",
 "synthesisCaution":"The 93% good-validity figure applies to ideal, well-lubricated and well-fitted use in recreational adults, so staff could assume the same agreement in field use with athletes.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Davarzani S, Helzer D, Rivera J, Saucier D, Jo E, Burch RF V, et al. Validity and Reliability of Strive Sense3 for Muscle Activity Monitoring During the Squat Exercise. Int J Kinesiology & Sports Sci. 2020;8(4):1-18.",
   "doi":"10.7575/aiac.ijkss.v.8n.4p.1",
   "abstract":"The Strive Sense3 smart-textile sEMG system was compared with a research-grade Noraxon system for rectus femoris activity during back squats at 30%, 60% and 80% of estimated 1RM in 17 participants. Correlation and ICC values were computed per trial. Results ranged from poor to excellent, with most trials good or better, and better agreement at medium and heavy loads. Outliers pointed to poor lubrication and fit. The authors conclude the system can track sEMG activity compared with a research-grade system.",
   "tldr":"The Strive Sense3 shorts tracked quadriceps activity reasonably well against a lab-grade EMG system in recreational adults doing squats, but only when the sensors were wet and fitted properly. Medium and heavy loads gave better agreement than light loads.",
   "methods":"Seventeen recreationally trained adults performed three continuous repetitions at each of 30%, 60% and 80% of estimated 1RM, with both systems recording rectus femoris sEMG concurrently. Signals were downsampled, time-aligned by cross-correlation, and analysed with Pearson r and a two-way mixed ICC for consistency. Five basketball coaches added an autoethnographic commentary.",
   "findings":"Correlation with the research-grade system was good or better in 93% of trials. Reliability was good or better in 87% of absolute sEMG trials and 98% of normalised trials. Outliers in participants 2, 10, 12, 13 and 15 were attributed to poor electrode contact or shorts fit. Medium and heavy loads gave higher validity and reliability than light loads.",
   "limitations":"Recreationally trained adults, not athletes. Data from participants 3 and 14 were excluded, and the device sampled at 21.33 Hz. The authors note the sensors must be lubricated before use. The coach commentary is autoethnographic, and one author has a former student employed by Strive.",
   "practicalImplications":"Lubricate sensor pads and check shorts fit before each session, since poor contact caused most outliers. Use the device for relative changes in quadriceps activity at medium to heavy loads, and read light-load data with more caution.",
   "athleteDev":"Check electrode contact and shorts fit before each squat session, and treat light-load data with caution. The study used recreational adults, so validity in athletes has not been tested.",
   "rtp":"The study does not address injury, recovery or return to sport, so it cannot be used to judge muscle readiness after injury."
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q40",
 "sourceFile":"Validity of force-velocity profiling assessed with a pneumatic leg press device.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title 'Validity of Force-Velocity Profiling Assessed With a Pneumatic Leg Press Device' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Methodological / Validation Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Research & Analytics","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Concurrent validity study of force-velocity variables from five Keiser pneumatic leg press units, compared with two force plates and a linear encoder, in 14 regularly active adults (mean age 29 years, 82 kg). Across 997 repetitions, average and peak force and velocity had correlations of 0.994 to 0.999 and coefficients of variation of 1.5% to 8.6%. Theoretical F0, V0, Pmax and force-velocity slope had correlations of 0.983 to 0.997 and coefficients of variation of 1.4% to 5.9%, while single-repetition power was less precise (CV 11.6% average, 17.2% peak).",
 "screeningLimitations":"Fourteen participants, with sex not reported, tested on one leg press model at Norwegian sports centres. The reference is device measurement (force plates and encoder), not athlete outcomes, so the paper does not show that profile values predict performance or change with training. The abstract gives a systematic bias of 0.7% to 7.1%, while the results give -8.4% to 4.7%; both are reported and the conflict is noted.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Good agreement across Keiser units does not make the values interchangeable with force-plate values or with vertical jump profiles, and single-repetition power should not be compared directly between athletes.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2021,
   "citation":"Lindberg K, Eythorsdottir I, Solberg P, Gløersen Ø, Seynnes O, Bjørnsen T, et al. Validity of Force-Velocity Profiling Assessed With a Pneumatic Leg Press Device. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2021 (ahead of print).",
   "doi":"10.1123/ijspp.2020-0954",
   "abstract":"Concurrent validity of force-velocity variables from five Keiser leg press devices was tested against two force plates and a linear encoder in 14 participants across 997 repetitions. Average and peak force and velocity agreed closely with reference measures. Extrapolated theoretical maximal force, velocity and power were precise, while single-repetition power was less precise. The authors recommend theoretical maximal power over single-repetition power.",
   "tldr":"Keiser pneumatic leg press data agreed closely with force plates and a linear encoder. The force-velocity profile (F0, V0, Pmax, slope) was more precise than single-repetition power, so use theoretical Pmax when profiling on this device.",
   "methods":"Fourteen regularly active participants completed 997 leg press repetitions across five Keiser units, with two force plates and a linear encoder recording at the same time. Protocol 1 used submaximal loads from 25 to 450 kgf in 14 participants; protocol 2 used maximal efforts across the Keiser 10-step test in 11 participants. Force-velocity profiles were fitted by linear regression for each participant and compared with reference data using bias, CV, correlation and ICC.",
   "findings":"Average and peak force and velocity correlated at 0.994 to 0.999 with coefficients of variation of 1.5% to 8.6%, and most biases were trivial to small. {
 "id":"Q41",
 "sourceFile":"Validity of research based on public data in sports medicine - A quantitative assessment of anterior cruciate ligament injuries in the NFL.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title 'Validity of Research Based on Public Data in Sports Medicine: A Quantitative Assessment of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in the National Football League' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"PRISMA systematic review of publicly obtained data (POD) studies of NFL musculoskeletal injuries published from 2000 to 2019, identifying 42 studies, 14 of them on ACL injuries. Each ACL study's count was compared with the ACL injuries in the NFL Injury Surveillance System for the same period. POD studies captured a mean of 66% of reported ACL injuries (range 31% to 90%), with 86% for skill players, 72% for midskill players, 61% for linemen and 35% for special teams injuries.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The comparison reference is the NFL injury surveillance database, which is not publicly available and depends on team reporting. Only what the published studies reported could be extracted, so player-level detail such as age and BMI could not be checked, and some studies grouped positions. Searches ended in June 2019 and were limited to English-language sources.",
 "synthesisCaution":"The 66% average capture rate spans 14 studies with a wide range, so staff should not use it as a correction factor to scale up injury counts from public-data studies.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2021,
   "citation":"Inclan PM, Chang PS, Mack CD, Solomon GS, Brophy RH, Hinton RY, et al. Validity of Research Based on Public Data in Sports Medicine: A Quantitative Assessment of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in the National Football League. Am J Sports Med. 2021:1-10.",
   "doi":"10.1177/03635465211015435",
   "abstract":"Systematic review of publicly obtained data studies of NFL injuries (42 studies, 14 on ACL injuries), with ACL injuries compared against the NFL Injury Surveillance System. Public-data studies captured a mean of 66% of ACL injuries, with capture varying by position and lowest on special teams. The authors conclude that these studies underreport injury incidence and favour more popular players.",
   "tldr":"Public-data NFL injury studies missed about a third of the ACL injuries teams reported to the league, with the largest gaps for linemen and special teams. Injury counts from public sources should be read as undercounts that favour popular players.",
   "methods":"PRISMA systematic review of English-language original research and grey literature on NFL injuries from public sources, searched in June 2019 across Medline, Embase, Scopus and ClinicalTrials.gov. Two reviewers screened records. Each ACL study's capture rate was its ACL injury count divided by the NFL surveillance count for the same period, with descriptive statistics for incidence and return to play.",
   "findings":"Of 42 POD studies, 35 (83%) were published in 2015 or later. Studies captured a mean of 66% of ACL injuries (range 31% to 90%). Capture was 86% for skill players, 72% for midskill players, 61% for linemen and 35% for special teams injuries. The authors conclude that the studies favour injuries in more popular players.",
   "limitations":"Comparison was limited to what the published studies reported, so player-level detail could not be checked. Some studies grouped positions, which affects position-level rates. Several authors have disclosed NFL consulting, grant or committee ties, and one is chair of the NFL Research and Innovation Committee.",
   "practicalImplications":"Treat injury counts drawn only from public media, fantasy sites or team reports as incomplete, especially for linemen and special teams. Use a standardised surveillance source when estimating incidence.",
   "athleteDev":"Do not use public-report injury counts to benchmark players or compare positions, because these sources miss injuries unevenly across positions.",
   "rtp":"The review addresses how injuries are counted, not how athletes recover, so it does not provide return-to-play outcomes or rates that staff can apply to an individual athlete."
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q42",
 "sourceFile":"Validity of the Elite HRV Smart Phone app for examining heart rate variability in a field based setting.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Manuscript title 'Validity of the Elite HRV Smart Phone Application for Examining Heart Rate Variability in a Field Based Setting' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Methodological / Validation Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Athletic Training","Research & Analytics","Coaching"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Female Athletes","Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Validation of the Elite HRV smartphone app against Kubios HRV 2.2 for log-transformed resting rMSSD, using R-R intervals from a Polar H7 recorded on waking for 14 consecutive days in 37 recreational athletes (29 men, 8 women; mean age 30.8 years) living in a dormitory. The two measures correlated strongly (r = 0.92, 95% CI 0.90 to 0.93), with a mean bias of -2.7% and 6.4% of residuals outside the limits of agreement (-12.0% to 7.0%). The authors conclude the app is not valid against Kubios.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Recording length varied beyond the planned 10 minutes because some participants lost track of time, and the app cannot select or trim segments, which the authors suggest may explain the disagreement. Only one heart rate monitor and one reference software were used, with no reliability testing. The sample was young, mostly male recreational athletes, so findings may not transfer to elite or female athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"A strong correlation (r = 0.92) does not mean the app's values match Kubios, because the bias and the wide limits of agreement mean the two cannot be used interchangeably.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2017,
   "citation":"Perrotta AS, Jeklin A, Hives BA, Meanwell LE, Warburton DER. Validity of the Elite HRV Smart Phone Application for Examining Heart Rate Variability in a Field Based Setting. J Strength Cond Res. 2017 (ahead of print).",
   "doi":"10.1519/JSC.0000000000001841",
   "abstract":"R-R intervals were recorded on waking for 14 days with the Elite HRV app and exported to Kubios HRV 2.2 for analysis. The app and Kubios rMSSD (log) correlated at r = 0.92, with a bias of -2.7% and 6.4% of residuals outside the limits of agreement. The authors judged the app not valid, and suggested it may be reliable rather than valid.",
   "tldr":"The Elite HRV app's rMSSD correlated strongly with Kubios (r = 0.92), but it read about 3% lower on average and 6% of readings fell outside the limits of agreement. The authors judged it not valid against Kubios and suggested it might be reliable, which this study did not test.",
   "methods":"Thirty-seven recreational athletes (29 men, 8 women; age 30.8 +/- 11.7 years) lived in a dormitory for 14 days and recorded resting R-R intervals with a Polar H7 on waking for about 10 minutes. Recordings were analysed in the Elite HRV app and exported to Kubios HRV 2.2. Log rMSSD from the two sources was compared by Pearson correlation and Bland-Altman analysis.",
   "findings":"The app and Kubios correlated at r = 0.92 (95% CI 0.90 to 0.93, P < 0.0001). The mean bias was -2.7% (95% CI -3.1 to -2.3%), with limits of agreement of -12.0% to 7.0% and 6.4% of residuals outside them. The authors state that the bias CI did not include the line of equality.",
   "limitations":"One heart rate monitor and one reference software were used, with no reliability testing. Recording durations varied beyond 10 minutes and the app cannot trim recordings. The sample was young and mostly male recreational athletes, so results may not transfer to elite or female athletes.",
   "practicalImplications":"Do not treat Elite HRV rMSSD values as interchangeable with Kubios values. Record for a fixed duration, as the authors advise, because variable recording lengths added to the disagreement.",
   "athleteDev":"Use this app's morning HRV readings with caution, since they run about 3% below Kubios on average with wide limits of agreement (-12% to +7%). Keep recordings to a fixed 10 minutes to reduce error.",
   "rtp":"The study addresses HRV measurement agreement in healthy recreational athletes. It does not assess injured or returning athletes and cannot inform return-to-sport decisions."
 }
}
